Diabetic retinopathy

No human PBM treatment study is listed. In diabetic animals, selected red or far-red protocols improved some retinal functional, vascular, or inflammatory measures, but results remain preclinical.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

No human PBM treatment study is listed. In diabetic animals, selected red or far-red protocols improved some retinal functional, vascular, or inflammatory measures, but results remain preclinical.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact diabetic-retinopathy category contains 11 publications: rat, mouse, and rabbit experiments plus retinal explant and cell work. Several reports combine animal and in-vitro methods, so type labels overlap. No direct human PBM treatment study appears in this category. The studies span different diabetes models, wavelengths, exposure schedules, and endpoints. Tang et al. 2013

Human and clinical evidence

No human clinical treatment study was identified in the source category. Evidence about retinal thickness, electroretinography, vascular leakage, or inflammatory markers therefore cannot be interpreted as a demonstrated improvement in patient vision or prevention of clinical diabetic retinopathy.

Animal evidence

Rat and mouse studies include streptozotocin-induced and genetic diabetes models. Several reports describe partial protection of retinal ganglion cells, photoreceptors, or retinal structure, and some report lower oxidative or inflammatory markers. Tang et al. found that daily 670 nm PBM at 6 J/cm² inhibited diabetes-associated retinal ganglion-cell loss and improved a photopic electroretinogram response in rats. A 2024 db/db mouse study used prolonged daily 654 nm exposure and reported changes in early retinal deterioration. Rabbit work tested a near-infrared emitting contact lens in diabetic retinopathy. The endpoints and animal models are not interchangeable.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Retinal explant and cultured-cell experiments examine high-glucose injury, mitochondrial changes, angiogenic signals, and inflammatory pathways. Some studies report protective changes, while one cell-signaling study describes trends that were not statistically clear. Laboratory findings remain mechanistic.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Reported wavelengths include 654, 670, and other red or near-infrared bands. Schedules range from brief daily irradiation to many hours per day for weeks or months. Methods, disease stage, and assessment times vary, and the source does not establish a clinically transferable dose.

Interpretation

There is a recurring preclinical signal for selected retinal outcomes, but no evidence here that PBM prevents vision loss or treats diabetic retinopathy in people. Human trials with clinically meaningful endpoints and well-defined dosing are needed before these findings can be generalized.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The exact category contains animal and laboratory research but no direct human treatment study. Several rodent experiments report structural, functional, vascular, or inflammatory changes with red or far-red light. A cell-signaling study reported trends without clear statistical support. Protocols and diabetes models vary.
